evidence.observation: The Settings interface enumerates every persisted setting. Fields that can be scoped to a project (e.g. defaultProvider, defaultModel, defaultThinkingLevel, theme, retry, compaction, terminal, defaultTools, sessionDir, extensions/skills/prompts/themes) sit alongside global-only fields, notably `defaultProjectTrust` (line 128, comment 'global setting only') and `cacheWarming` (line 157, comment 'global only because each refresh costs money'). This defines which keys participate in the user/project merge and which are read only from the user scope.

deepMergeSettings(base, overrides) delegates to deepMergeObjects. Its doc comment states 'project/overrides take precedence, nested objects merge recursively'. deepMergeObjects (lines 169-186) skips `undefined` override values, so an unset higher-precedence layer does not clobber a lower one, and recurses only for plain objects while arrays are replaced wholesale. This is the primitive that makes precedence per-field with recursive nested-object merging.

The SettingsManager constructor stores the two loaded scopes (this.globalSettings, this.projectSettings) and then computes the effective settings exactly once as `this.settings = deepMergeSettings(this.globalSettings, this.projectSettings)` (line 350). The base layer is the user/agent-dir settings and the override layer is project settings, which fixes user < project in the merge order. getGlobalSettings()/getProjectSettings() (lines 502-508) expose the pre-merge scopes via structuredClone.

loadFromStorage is the per-scope loader. Its first branch short-circuits: `if (scope === "project" && !projectTrusted) return {}` (lines 411-413), so untrusted project settings contribute nothing and cannot override user settings. Otherwise it reads the storage contents under a lock, returns {} when empty, and parses via migrateSettings. fromStorageWithPaths (lines 380-407) calls it for 'global' first and 'project' second, confirming user scope is the merge base loaded before the project scope.

applyOverrides(overrides) computes `this.settings = deepMergeSettings(this.settings, overrides)` (line 569). Because it merges onto the already-merged user+project result, any value passed here is the highest-precedence settings layer short of a dedicated CLI flag path. It is the runtime hook used for CLI-derived settings overrides, and unlike save()/updateProjectSettings it never persists.

getDefaultProjectTrust reads `this.globalSettings.defaultProjectTrust` directly rather than `this.settings`, then validates the value and falls back to "ask". This is the concrete pattern for global-only settings: project settings are deliberately excluded from the lookup, and a built-in default is the final fallback. getCacheWarmingMode (lines 955-958) applies the same global-only + default pattern.

getClearOnShrink documents and implements a three-tier lookup: the merged settings value wins when defined ('Settings takes precedence, then env var, then default false'), otherwise the PI_CLEAR_ON_SHRINK environment variable, otherwise false. Many getters follow the same `merged setting ?? built-in literal` fallback shape, e.g. getCompactionEnabled (`?? true`, line 846), getTransport (`?? "auto"`, line 836), and getRetrySettings (lines 932-939).

resolveConfigValue resolves a single configured value (API key, header, proxy, etc.) and encodes its internal precedence in the doc comment: a leading '!' executes the remainder as a shell command and uses cached stdout; otherwise the value is parsed as a template and '$ENV_VAR'/'${ENV_VAR}' references are interpolated from the environment; '$$' and '$!' escape literals; anything else is a literal. This is a value-resolution ladder (command > env interpolation > literal) that runs on the string that already won the settings merge.

parseConfigValueReference is the branch point that classifies a config string: `config.startsWith("!")` yields a `{ type: "command" }` reference (highest precedence, shell execution), otherwise a `{ type: "template", parts }` reference parsed by parseConfigValueTemplate (lines 29-77). Because the classification is purely prefix-based, a '!' value always beats an env-var reference regardless of the settings layer that supplied it.

resolveEnvConfigValue(name, env) returns `env?.[name] || process.env[name] || undefined`: an explicitly supplied env map (e.g. an SDK/test override or provider-specific environment) takes precedence over the ambient process.env, and an unresolved variable returns undefined. resolveTemplate (lines 101-113) then fails the whole template (returns undefined) if any required env part is missing, so partial interpolation never silently succeeds.

getConfigValueEnvVarName reports the single environment variable backing a pure '$VAR' template and returns undefined for shell-command values or multi-part templates. Together with getConfigValueEnvVarNames (lines 121-124) and getMissingConfigValueEnvVarNames (lines 126-128) it lets callers decide 'is this value configured?' via isConfigValueConfigured (lines 132-134) without executing commands, which is how the auth/model layers distinguish a missing literal from a missing environment reference.

buildSessionOptions demonstrates CLI-over-settings precedence for session options. `--thinking` explicitly overwrites any thinking level derived from settings-scoped models ('Thinking level from CLI (takes precedence over scoped model thinking levels set above)', lines 514-517); `--model`/`--provider` populate options.model before saved settings defaults are consulted (lines 468-503); and `--tools`/`--exclude-tools`/`--no-tools` overwrite the defaultTools setting (lines 534-542).

The session-directory lookup is an explicit CLI > env > settings > default ladder: `(parsed.sessionDir ? normalizePath(parsed.sessionDir) : undefined) ?? (envSessionDir ? expandTildePath(envSessionDir) : undefined) ?? startupSettingsManager.getSessionDir()`. The `??` chain only reaches the merged settings value (and ultimately the manager's internal default) when neither the CLI flag nor PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR is set.

In interactive mode, `--use-theme` is applied through `startupSettingsManager.applyOverrides({ theme: parsed.useTheme })`, routing a CLI value through the highest settings layer so it overlays the user+project merge without being written to disk. This is the concrete CLI-settings path for the applyOverrides mechanism.

The settings reference states the intended ordering: 'Project settings override agent-directory settings. Resource lists are combined.' It also flags global-only settings (defaultProjectTrust 'Can only be set in agent-directory settings') and CLI overrides (defaultTools: 'CLI tool options override this setting for one invocation'), matching the implementation in settings-manager.ts.

claims.claim: User/agent-directory settings are loaded as the base layer and project (.pi) settings are loaded as the override layer; the effective settings are computed as deepMergeSettings(globalSettings, projectSettings), so project values win over user values per field.

The merge is per-field and recursive over plain nested objects: deepMergeObjects ignores undefined overrides (so lower layers survive when a higher layer does not set a key) and replaces arrays wholesale rather than concatenating them.

Project settings are only applied when the project is trusted: loadFromStorage returns {} for the 'project' scope when projectTrusted is false, so an untrusted repository cannot override user settings.

CLI/runtime overrides occupy the highest settings layer: applyOverrides deep-merges a Partial<Settings> on top of the already-merged global+project settings without persisting it, and main.ts uses it for --use-theme via startupSettingsManager.applyOverrides({ theme: parsed.useTheme }).

Built-in defaults form the lowest layer and are expressed as ?? fallbacks inside the SettingsManager getters (e.g. compaction.enabled ?? true, retry.maxRetries ?? 3, transport ?? "auto"), applied only after the CLI, project, and user layers are exhausted.

Some environment variables participate between settings and defaults; getClearOnShrink resolves merged settings first, then PI_CLEAR_ON_SHRINK, then false, and getExternalEditorCommand resolves the externalEditor setting, then VISUAL/EDITOR, then the platform default.

Certain settings are user-scope only and deliberately ignore project settings: getDefaultProjectTrust reads this.globalSettings.defaultProjectTrust (falling back to "ask") and getCacheWarmingMode reads this.globalSettings.cacheWarming (falling back to "streaming"), bypassing the merged this.settings.

For individual config values, resolveConfigValue applies a resolution ladder independent of the settings file merge: a leading '!' shell command (cached) takes precedence over '$VAR'/'${VAR}' environment interpolation, which takes precedence over a plain literal.

Environment interpolation itself has a precedence order: an explicitly supplied env map is consulted before process.env, and if any referenced variable is undefined the whole templated value fails to resolve (returns undefined) rather than partially interpolating.

Session directory selection is an explicit CLI > environment > merged settings > default ladder in main.ts: parsed.sessionDir ?? PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR ?? settingsManager.getSessionDir(), with the settings lookup reached only when the two higher layers are unset.

CLI flags for session options override settings-derived values: --thinking overrides scoped-model thinking levels and settings defaults, --model/--provider are resolved before saved defaultProvider/defaultModel are consulted, and --tools/--exclude-tools/--no-tools override the defaultTools setting for one invocation.

conclusion.summary: Settings in packages/coding-agent/src/core resolve through four layers, from lowest to highest precedence: (1) built-in defaults hard-coded as ?? fallbacks in SettingsManager getters and constants such as DEFAULT_COMPACTION_TOKEN_SETTINGS; (2) user/agent-directory settings from <agent-dir>/settings.json (~/.pi/agent/settings.json), loaded as globalSettings; (3) project settings from <cwd>/.pi/settings.json, loaded as projectSettings only when the project is trusted and otherwise treated as {}; the effective value is deepMergeSettings(globalSettings, projectSettings), a per-field recursive merge where project wins on scalars/arrays and nested objects merge; (4) CLI/runtime overrides, which sit on top via applyOverrides (e.g. --use-theme) or are injected as session options/derived values (--model/--provider/--thinking/--tools/--session-dir) before settings-derived defaults are consulted.

precedence_table.source: Hard-coded fallbacks in SettingsManager getters plus DEFAULT_COMPACTION_TOKEN_SETTINGS / DEFAULT_HTTP_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS; documented 'Default' column in docs/settings.md
<cwd>/.pi/settings.json, loaded as projectSettings only when trusted, then merged over the user scope
applyOverrides({...}) on the merged settings (e.g. --use-theme) and CLI session options (--model/--provider/--thinking/--tools/--session-dir) that beat settings-derived values

exceptions: Global-only settings bypass the project layer: getDefaultProjectTrust (lines 1031-1034) and getCacheWarmingMode (lines 955-958) read this.globalSettings directly.
Untrusted projects contribute no settings at all (loadFromStorage returns {} for scope "project").

Environment variables slot between settings and defaults for some keys (getClearOnShrink lines 1235-1241; getExternalEditorCommand lines 986-996; getShowHardwareCursor line 1358) and, for sessionDir, the env var sits above settings but below the CLI flag.

Within a resolved config-value string, resolveConfigValue applies a separate ladder: shell command (! prefix) > env interpolation ($VAR/${VAR}) > literal, with an explicit env map taking precedence over process.env.
